This vignette introduces the general ADMG identification tools in
`CausalGraphs.jl`. The key distinction is between two related tasks:

1. deciding whether a causal effect is identified from an ADMG;
2. choosing an estimator that is already implemented in the package.

`identify()` is the estimator-routing function. It first checks the effect
classes for which `estimate_causal()` has estimators: a-fixable, p-fixable, and
nested-fixable effects. `ID_algorithm()` is the more general symbolic
Pearl-Shpitser ID check for ADMG total-effect queries.

## Setup

```{julia}
import Pkg
Pkg.activate(joinpath(@__DIR__, ".."); io=devnull)

using CausalGraphs
```

## Front-Door as a General ID Query

The front-door graph has an unmeasured common cause of treatment and outcome,
represented by `A <-> Y`, but the causal effect of `A` on `Y` is still
identified through the mediator `M`.

```{julia}
g_fd = make_graph(
    vertices = [:A, :M, :Y],
    di_edges = [(:A, :M), (:M, :Y)],
    bi_edges = [(:A, :Y)],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(g_fd; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

For estimation, this graph is p-fixable, so `identify()` routes to the NPS-TMLE
estimator.

```{julia}
identify(g_fd, :A, :Y).strategy
```

The same graph is also identified by the general ID algorithm. Here
`ID_algorithm()` returns a symbolic functional.

```{julia}
id_fd = ID_algorithm(g_fd, :A, :Y)
println("identified: ", id_fd.identified)
println("functional: ", id_fd.expression)
```

The printed expression is intentionally compact. In the front-door graph it is
the familiar formula: average the mediator distribution under the intervention,
then average the mediator-outcome regression over the observed treatment
distribution.

## Non-Identification and Hedges

The bow graph is the simplest non-identified ADMG for the effect of `A` on `Y`.
It has both a causal edge `A -> Y` and hidden confounding `A <-> Y`. The
observed association cannot separate the directed effect from the latent common
cause.

```{julia}
g_bow = make_graph(
    vertices = [:A, :Y],
    di_edges = [(:A, :Y)],
    bi_edges = [(:A, :Y)],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(g_bow; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

```{julia}
id_bow = ID_algorithm(g_bow, :A, :Y)
println("identified: ", id_bow.identified)
println("hedge:      ", id_bow.hedge)
```

When ID fails, the returned hedge is a graph-theoretic witness of
non-identification. In practice, this is more useful than a bare `false`
because it points to the district structure responsible for the failure.

## Fixing Sequences

Fixing is the graph operation that turns random vertices into intervention-like
or conditioned-on vertices by removing incoming directed edges and bidirected
edges involving the fixed node. A vertex is fixable when it is not in the same
district as one of its proper descendants.

The helper `fixing_sequence()` tries to fix a requested set of nodes and
returns the order it found.

```{julia}
g_bd = make_graph(
    vertices = [:X, :A, :Y],
    di_edges = [(:X, :A), (:X, :Y), (:A, :Y)],
);

fixing_sequence(g_bd, [:A])
```

For the backdoor graph, fixing `A` succeeds immediately because `A` is not
bidirected-connected to its descendant `Y`.

## Nested-Fixability Diagnostics

Nested-fixability uses fixing operations inside induced subgraphs. It is more
general than ordinary backdoor adjustment and p-fixability, and it underlies the
ANIPW/NIPW estimator route in this package.

The graph below is not p-fixable because `A` and its child `M` are in the same
district. The nested check exposes the SWIG ancestor set and the fixing
diagnostics used by `identify()`.

```{julia}
g_nested = make_graph(
    vertices = [:Z, :A, :M, :Y],
    di_edges = [(:Z, :A), (:Z, :Y), (:A, :M), (:M, :Y)],
    bi_edges = [(:A, :M)],
);

println("p-fixable: ", is_p_fix(g_nested, :A))
nested = nested_fixability(g_nested, :A, :Y)
println("nested identified: ", nested.identified)
println("Y*:               ", nested.ystar)
println("nested order:     ", nested.n_order)
```

The nested diagnostics are useful when building or debugging examples. They
show which outcome ancestors remain after fixing treatment and which districts
must be reachable by fixing vertices outside the district.

## How the Pieces Fit Together

Use the functions at different levels of generality:

- `is_fix()` and `is_p_fix()` are simple graph checks.
- `nested_fixability()` explains the nested/fixing route used by the ANIPW
  estimator.
- `ID_algorithm()` answers the more general symbolic ADMG identification
  question and returns a hedge when the effect is not identified.
- `identify()` combines these checks for package routing.
- `estimate_causal()` estimates only the currently implemented estimator
  classes: a-fixable, p-fixable, and nested-fixable.

This separation is deliberate. General ID can produce complicated functionals.
Those functionals are useful identification results, but they require separate
estimation machinery before they should be treated as automatic estimators.
